system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
# Project Kestrel: Buyer Review of Seller Update and Disclosure Letter (SPA-003)

## Headline view

The Seller says the package is "fair and balanced." It is not. Taken together, the positions shift almost every known risk back onto Wattlebridge:

- known, quantified liabilities are left out of the price mechanics;
- title and capacity protection is weakened;
- the Buyer's knowledge of the data room would be used to defeat claims about the very issues the data room reveals.

The Seller's own Disclosure Letter also contradicts several statements in its covering Update. Bluefen, Riverlark and the bonuses are the clearest examples. We should point this out directly in our response.

I have not seen the full SPA, so clause references follow the Seller's numbering. Before you circulate this, NSW/Australian counsel should confirm the law-specific points below (Privacy Act, ACL, tax amendment periods, payroll tax).

---

## Part A: Structural issues with the limitations regime

### 1. Limitations applied to "all Claims of any nature" (Cl 12.3/13, 9.3, 12.8, 20.5)
**Problem.** The proposals that "any limitation applies to all Claims unless expressly stated otherwise" and that exclusive-remedy and non-reliance apply to "all Claims of any nature" would extend the cap, basket, de minimis and 18-month limit to:
- specific indemnities;
- tax claims;
- breach of covenant;
- leakage and price-adjustment claims;
- arguably fraud.

This guts every specific protection we negotiate.

**Push back.**
- Invert the default. Limitations apply to **general Warranty Claims only**, unless expressly extended.
- Carve out fraud, dishonesty and wilful concealment from all limitations, and from non-reliance and exclusive remedy.
- Exclusive remedy must not restrict specific performance, injunctions, pre-Completion termination rights, the price-adjustment mechanism or indemnities.
- Non-reliance should be limited to statements outside the SPA and Disclosure Letter. It should not purport to exclude claims for misleading conduct arising from the Seller's own deliberate statements. Australian courts treat such clauses as relevant but not conclusive under the ACL, so the Seller gains little legitimate protection from the broad form anyway.

### 2. Fundamental (title and capacity) warranties under the general cap and time limit
**Problem.** Title is the whole deal. If title fails, the Buyer has lost AUD 24m, yet recovery would be capped at AUD 4.8m and barred after 18 months. "Administrative simplicity" is not a reason.

**Push back.**
- Title, capacity, authority and solvency warranties are capped at 100% of the price.
- No de minimis or basket applies to them.
- The time limit is the statutory limitation period (or 7 years).
- They are not qualified by disclosure or Buyer knowledge.

### 3. Title evidenced only by the DD-012 share register
**Problem.** The register is the Company's own internal record. The Seller's letter (item 10) expressly notes the Buyer has not verified it. The Riverlark facility also raises a real risk that the shares are secured, for example by a share mortgage or an all-assets security interest granted by the Seller.

**Push back and diligence.**
- ASIC company extract reconciled to the register.
- PPSR searches against the Seller and the Company.
- Constitution review covering pre-emption and transfer restrictions, with waivers delivered.
- Confirmation that there are no options, convertible notes, SAFEs or ESOP entitlements. This matters for a VC-held company.
- Share certificates, signed transfer forms and board approvals as Completion deliverables.
- A full release of any security over the shares at Completion.

### 4. General disclosure of the entire data room and public registers (Disclosure Letter 1.1–1.2; Schedule 7)
**Problem.** Disclosing everything "contained or referred to" in the data room, the Accounts and "publicly searchable corporate records" means the Buyer must hunt for issues. Effectively, any document anywhere qualifies every warranty.

**Push back.**
- Only specific disclosures qualify warranties.
- Each disclosure must be fair: enough detail for a buyer to identify the nature, scope and likely financial effect of the matter.
- Delete general data-room disclosure. At most, allow disclosure of the contents of named documents against specified warranties.
- Limit public-register disclosure to ASIC and PPSR searches against the Company on a stated date.
- Disclosure must never qualify fundamental warranties, tax warranties or indemnities.
- Item 1.4 (non-admission) is acceptable only if it cannot be read to dilute specific disclosures.

### 5. Buyer knowledge exclusion (Cl 8.3)
**Problem.** This is the most dangerous clause in the package. It covers knowledge of the Buyer or its advisers, including anything "discoverable" from the data room or public records. Read with the general disclosure, it means every issue this memo identifies would be unclaimable because we found it. It would also defeat any specific indemnity, since indemnities exist precisely because the Buyer knows of the issue.

**Push back.**
- Delete. Our preferred position is an express pro-sandbagging clause: Buyer knowledge does not limit claims.
- Fallback: limit it to the actual knowledge of named individuals on the Wattlebridge deal team, of matters fairly disclosed.
- Exclude constructive or imputed knowledge and advisers' knowledge.
- Never apply it to fundamental warranties, tax or indemnities.

### 6. Cap, de minimis and basket (Cl 12.1–12.2)
**Assessment.** A 20% cap (AUD 4.8m) for general warranties is within market range. The AUD 250,000 basket (about 1% of price) operating as a deductible ("only the excess") is Seller-favourable.

**Push back.**
- Basket at about 0.5% (AUD 120,000), on a tipping basis so that once exceeded, the full amount is recoverable.
- De minimis of AUD 10,000–15,000, with related claims aggregated.
- Consider asking for a cap of 25–30%, or using warranty and indemnity (W&I) insurance with a Seller retention. If W&I is used, the specific known issues below will be excluded by the insurer, so they **must** sit in Seller-backed specific indemnities.

### 7. Time limits (Cl 12.3/13)
- 18 months for general warranties is acceptable. It covers one full audit cycle.
- Tax warranties and the tax indemnity need a separate regime: at least 5 years, or 3 months after the relevant ATO amendment period expires, with no limit for fraud or evasion. "Settled under the general regime" is not acceptable.
- IP warranties should run at least 3–4 years, given the Ironquay issue.

### 8. Stale disclosure date
The letter speaks as at **22 September 2026**. It is now 6 November 2026, so six weeks of developments are undisclosed, including on Bluefen and the incident.

**Push back.**
- Require an updated disclosure letter before signing.
- Any disclosure against warranties repeated at Completion must not cure breaches.
- If a supplemental disclosure reveals a material matter, the Buyer should be entitled to terminate or claim.

---

## Part B: Specific known issues (price, conditions and indemnities)

These are known, identified risks. They belong in the price mechanics, conditions precedent and specific indemnities that sit **outside** the cap, basket, de minimis, time limit, disclosure and knowledge limitations. They should not be left to general warranties.

### 9. Riverlark facility (~AUD 3.2m): release "following Completion"
**Problem.** This is inconsistent with a debt-free/cash-free deal. The Disclosure Letter (item 3) confirms the facility is not repaid and no discharge is in the data room. The change-control clause (8.1) may trigger default or acceleration at Completion. A post-Completion release leaves the Buyer owning a company with live security, and possibly encumbered shares, relying on Seller goodwill.

**Push back.**
- Repayment **at Completion**, paid directly from the purchase price to Riverlark under a payout letter that states the exact figure, including interest, break costs and fees.
- Completion deliverables: a deed of release and PPSR financing change statements, or an undertaking to lodge them within 1–2 business days.
- The full payout amount is treated as Debt and deducted from the price.
- Replace "approximately" with a confirmed figure.

### 10. Bluefen change-control consent (~AUD 3.6m, ~30% of revenue)
**Problem.**
- The Update says this is "addressed," but the letter (item 2) confirms there is no final consent and no evidence that the clause 11.3 conditions are satisfied.
- "Reasonable endeavours" is weak.
- Treating the condition as satisfied on "delivery of written consent" would capture a consent that imposes new conditions, price changes or amended terms.

**Push back.**
- Condition precedent: Bluefen's written consent, unconditional or on terms approved by the Buyer (acting reasonably), with all clause 11.3 conditions satisfied and no adverse change to the contract.
- The Buyer approves the form of consent.
- The Seller uses all reasonable or best endeavours, and the Buyer may participate in communications with Bluefen.
- The condition is waivable **only by the Buyer**.
- Sunset date with a Buyer termination right.
- Consider protection if Bluefen terminates or materially reduces volumes within 12 months citing the change of control. This could be a specific indemnity, a price adjustment or deferred consideration, given that 30% of revenue is concentrated in one customer.

### 11. DD-005 Completion bonuses (AUD 420,000 plus on-costs)
**Problem.** "A matter for the Seller" is wrong if the **Company** is the paying entity. These are transaction-triggered liabilities of the target. Leaving them out of the funds flow means the Buyer effectively funds them on top of the price. Payroll tax, superannuation guarantee and PAYG withholding are unaddressed (item 5). NSW payroll tax and the SG rate of 12% may apply, depending on how the bonuses are characterised. If the continued-employment conditions run past Completion, the liability will crystallise on the Buyer's watch.

**Push back.**
- Treat the bonuses plus all on-costs (payroll tax, super, workers compensation, PAYG) as Debt or Transaction Costs, deducted from the price.
- Either pay them through the Company's payroll at Completion, or hold a retention amount for any post-Completion instalments.
- Specific indemnity for any shortfall or associated claims.
- The funds flow must itemise them.

### 12. Ironquay IP: SOW3 Project Materials
**Problem.** Under DD-004 clause 7.3, the IP in the SOW3 materials does **not** transfer until every SOW3 fee has cleared. DD-010 shows AUD 180,000 open, and there is no receipt or confirmatory assignment. The Company may not own IP that may be core to the product. An indemnity "limited to the SOW3 payment" covers the AUD 180,000 debt but none of the real risks:
- ownership failure;
- infringement claims by Ironquay;
- injunctions;
- redevelopment cost;
- loss of customer contracts that depend on the IP.

**Push back.**
- Completion deliverables: evidence of cleared payment, or payment from the purchase price with the amount treated as Debt; a confirmatory IP assignment deed from Ironquay; and moral rights consents.
- Specific uncapped (or price-capped) indemnity covering all loss from the Company not owning, or being unable to use, the SOW3 materials, outside all limitations.
- IP warranties are not "settled." We need full ownership and non-infringement warranties with an extended time limit.

### 13. DD-006 export and privacy incident (~1,240 records)
**Problem.** The Seller says this is "not expected to be material." That is an assertion, not a warranty, and it conflicts with the letter (item 6): access, scope and notification obligations are all unresolved and the investigation is "preliminary."

The issues are:
- Paperbark's revenue (around AUD 12m implied by the Bluefen figure) appears to place it outside the small business exemption, so the Privacy Act and Notifiable Data Breaches scheme likely apply.
- The scheme requires a reasonable, expeditious assessment within 30 days. Given the 22 September letter date, that window has likely passed, so we need to know whether an assessment was completed.
- Exposure includes OAIC action under the enhanced penalty regime, the statutory privacy tort, and contractual notification obligations to customers, possibly including Bluefen.

**Push back.**
- Pre-Completion covenants: complete a forensic investigation by an independent provider, give the Buyer full information rights, and make any required OAIC or individual notifications.
- Warranty that the investigation and assessment were properly conducted.
- Specific indemnity for all incident-related loss (regulatory, third-party, customer, remediation, notification costs), outside the cap, thresholds, knowledge and disclosure limitations, for at least 3 years.
- Consider a retention amount to back it.

### 14. Sandbar supplier renewals (3 × AUD 110,000 = AUD 330,000)
**Problem.** The letter itself flags these as "related," to be "read together for timing/scope." That is a classic sign of a commitment split to stay below an approval or materiality threshold, for example a conduct-of-business consent threshold or the "Material Contract" definition. The letter does not say whether they are unavoidable, terminable, accrued or in the ordinary course. Calling them "ordinary-course operating costs" is the Seller's characterisation, not a fact.

**Push back and diligence.**
- Obtain all three contracts and the approval trail.
- Confirm whether Sandbar is a related party of the Seller or management.
- Confirm termination rights, and whether the amounts are accrued in the Accounts or working capital.
- Aggregate related contracts for all thresholds in the SPA.
- If entered outside the ordinary course or without required approval, require termination before Completion at the Seller's cost, or treat the amounts as Debt or leakage.
- Arm's-length and related-party warranty.

### 15. Office lease (DD-007) and Mossvale (DD-009): lower priority
- **Lease:** make landlord notification a Seller covenant or Completion deliverable, and confirm independently that no consent is triggered.
- **Mossvale:** confirm legally whether the assignment restriction treats a change of control as an assignment. If unclear, obtain a comfort letter or consent.
- In both cases, the Disclosure Letter's wording ("does not describe it as…", "does not state…") is carefully non-committal. Do not rely on it as a conclusion.

---

## Part C: Credit risk on the Seller
Harbourglass Ventures is a VC vehicle and is likely to distribute proceeds quickly. Even well-drafted indemnities are worth little against an empty Seller.

**Recommend:**
- a retention or escrow of about AUD 2.0–2.4m (8–10% of price) for 18–24 months, to back the specific indemnities;
- and/or a parent or fund guarantee;
- alternatively, W&I insurance for general warranties plus a retention for the specific indemnities, which W&I will exclude.

---

## Summary of recommendations

| Priority | Issue | Seller position | Buyer response |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Critical** | Limitations scope (12.3/9.3/12.8/20.5) | Apply to all Claims | General warranties only; carve out fraud, indemnities, tax, covenants and price mechanics |
| **Critical** | Buyer knowledge (8.3) | Actual and constructive knowledge bars claims | Delete; pro-sandbagging. Fallback: named individuals' actual knowledge only |
| **Critical** | General disclosure | Whole data room and public records | Specific, fair disclosure only; never against fundamentals, tax or indemnities |
| **Critical** | Fundamental/title warranties | Same cap and time as general | 100% cap, no thresholds, statutory period; independent title verification |
| **Critical** | Riverlark (~AUD 3.2m) | Release post-Completion | Repay from price at Completion; payout letter, deed of release, PPSR discharge; treat as Debt |
| **Critical** | Bluefen (30% revenue) | Reasonable endeavours; any written consent | Buyer-approved unconditional consent as condition precedent; Buyer-only waiver; sunset; revenue protection |
| **High** | Bonuses (AUD 420k plus on-costs) | Seller's matter; omitted from funds flow | Debt or Transaction Cost incl. payroll tax and super; itemise; indemnify |
| **High** | Ironquay IP | Indemnity limited to SOW3 payment | Payment plus confirmatory assignment at Completion; full IP indemnity; extended IP warranties |
| **High** | DD-006 privacy incident | "Not material" | Forensic completion, notification covenants, uncapped-style specific indemnity, retention |
| **High** | Tax | General regime | Separate tax indemnity; time limit tied to ATO amendment periods |
| **Medium** | Sandbar renewals (AUD 330k) | Ordinary course | Diligence related-party status and splitting; aggregate thresholds; Debt or terminate if improper |
| **Medium** | Cap and thresholds | 20%; AUD 25k; AUD 250k deductible | Basket ~AUD 120k tipping; de minimis AUD 10–15k with aggregation; consider 25–30% cap or W&I |
| **Medium** | Stale disclosure (22 Sep) | – | Updated letter before signing; Completion disclosures do not cure |
| **Medium** | Seller credit risk | – | Escrow or retention of ~AUD 2.0–2.4m and/or a guarantee |
| **Low** | Lease and Mossvale | Not consent triggers | Verify independently; notification covenant; comfort letter if unclear |

**Overall approach.** Accept a market-standard general warranty regime (a 20% cap and 18 months are negotiable starting points). In return, hold firm that the known issues are dealt with through the price (Riverlark, bonuses, Ironquay fee, possibly Sandbar), conditions precedent (Bluefen) and ring-fenced specific indemnities backed by a retention (Ironquay IP, privacy incident, tax). Those protections must not be undermined by general disclosure, Buyer knowledge or the "all Claims" limitation language.

If helpful, I can next prepare a clause-by-clause mark-up response or a short issues list for the Seller.
=== END ADVICE ===
